title: Tension headaches that won't go away
intro: A dull, band-like ache across the forehead or the back of the head that shows up most days and never fully lifts is one of the most common reasons people search for headache relief. It's usually filed under "tension headache" and treated as a stress or posture problem.

The standard advice is reasonable as a starting point: drink enough water, take regular breaks from screens, try an OTC pain reliever, manage stress. For a lot of people that's enough. For others, none of it moves the needle, and the headache just keeps coming back.

sections.heading: The Hypermobility Link Behind Chronic Tension Headaches
body: We're not doctors, and this isn't medical advice. It's a summary of what the published research says about a piece of the picture that often gets skipped: the neck.

In hypermobility studies, headache and neck pain show up together often. Malhotra et al. (2020), a retrospective review of 140 patients with hypermobility disorders at a single center, found that 66% reported headache or neck pain and 53% reported both together; migraine was the most common headache type, found in 83% of those with headache. A 2024 review in Frontiers in Neurology on headache disorders in EDS and hypermobility spectrum disorders put migraine prevalence estimates across the broader literature at 40% to 75%, well above the roughly 14% rate seen in the general population.

There's a mechanical explanation for why neck problems can produce headaches, and it points specifically at cervicogenic headache (a headache caused directly by a problem in the neck), not at tension-type headache in general. Zito, Jull, and Story (Manual Therapy, 2006) compared 27 people with cervicogenic headache, 25 with migraine, and 25 pain-free controls, and found that manual examination of the upper neck joints could pick out the cervicogenic headache group from the other two with 80% sensitivity. A larger follow-up by Jull and colleagues (Cephalalgia, 2007), testing 73 people with a single headache type (migraine, tension-type, or cervicogenic) against 57 controls, found the same pattern: restricted neck movement, painful upper cervical joint dysfunction, and weak deep neck flexor muscles identified the cervicogenic headache group with 100% sensitivity and 94% specificity. That study found no evidence of this cervical impairment pattern in the migraine or tension-type headache groups. The mechanical neck problem tracks specifically with cervicogenic headache, not with ordinary tension-type headache.

That's a useful distinction for anyone whose headache has been labeled "tension-type" by default: cervicogenic headache can look and feel similar day to day, but it has an identifiable, mechanical cause in the neck, and standard tension-headache advice won't necessarily touch it. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis pooling 77 studies and over 2,500 participants did find some cervical musculoskeletal differences, like forward head posture and reduced neck rotation, in people with migraine and tension-type headache too, but rated that evidence as very low certainty and not always clinically meaningful. No study has yet tested the specific question of tension-type headache within a confirmed hEDS or HSD population, so the neck-headache mechanism is well established in general headache research, but how often it plays out inside hypermobile joints specifically is still an open question.

bridge_to_hub: Neck Instability and Cervical Pain; Chronic Migraines
action_title: What to bring to a doctor
action_body: If a headache has resisted the usual fixes, it's worth describing the neck alongside it: stiffness, a sense of instability, or pain that worsens with certain head positions. A doctor or physical therapist can assess cervical joint and muscle function directly to check specifically for cervicogenic headache, which isn't something that shows up on a standard headache workup. Our Neck Instability and Cervical Pain page and our Chronic Migraines page go into more depth on what that assessment can look like and what the hypermobility research says about each.

sources.text: Malhotra et al., 'Headaches in hypermobility syndromes: a pain in the neck?,' American Journal of Medical Genetics Part A, 2020 (n=140)
Mehta et al., 'Headache disorders in patients with Ehlers-Danlos syndromes and hypermobility spectrum disorders,' Frontiers in Neurology, 2024
Zito, Jull & Story, 'Clinical tests of musculoskeletal dysfunction in the diagnosis of cervicogenic headache,' Manual Therapy, 2006;11(2):118-129 (n=77)
Jull, Amiri, Bullock-Saxton, Darnell & Lander, 'Cervical musculoskeletal impairment in frequent intermittent headache. Part 1: subjects with single headaches,' Cephalalgia, 2007;27(7):793-802 (n=130)

Systematic review and meta-analysis, 'Cervical musculoskeletal impairments in migraine and tension-type headache and relationship to pain related factors,' Musculoskeletal Science and Practice, 2025 (77 studies, n=2,551)

title: Why do I bruise so easily
intro: A bruise that shows up from a bump you barely felt, or one that seems way out of proportion to whatever caused it, is a common enough complaint that most people brush it off as clumsiness or just how their skin is.
Vitamin deficiencies, blood thinners, and aging skin are the usual explanations doctors check first, and for many people one of those accounts for it.

sections.heading: The Hypermobility Link Behind Easy Bruising
body: We're not doctors. Here's what a 2023 clinical review in JAAD found, pooling data across 140 studies and 839 patients: easy bruising and skin fragility show up consistently across Ehlers-Danlos syndrome subtypes. The review doesn't pin the mechanism down to anything more specific than connective tissue differences, so that's as far as the evidence goes. Anything more detailed than that is speculation, not something the research has confirmed.

For people who do notice this pattern, the Ehlers-Danlos Society's skin care guidance is worth knowing about: fragrance-free gentle cleansers, lukewarm rather than hot water, daily SPF, and silicone gel or sheets for scarring after skin injuries.

action_title: What to bring to a doctor
action_body: If bruising has been a lifelong pattern rather than something new, it's worth mentioning alongside any joint symptoms when talking to a doctor, since the two can point to the same underlying connective tissue picture. Our Skin Fragility and Easy Bruising page covers the fuller research and the skin care guidance in more depth.

sources.text: JAAD 2023 clinical review, skin fragility and bruising across EDS subtypes (839 patients, 140 pooled studies)

title: Why do I feel dizzy when I stand up
intro: Standing up too fast and feeling the room tilt, sometimes with a pounding heartbeat, is common enough to have a name most people already know: getting up too quickly, low blood pressure, needing more water or salt.
Those explanations are worth ruling out first, and simple fixes like standing up slower or staying hydrated genuinely help a lot of people.

sections.heading: The Hypermobility Link Behind Standing Dizziness (POTS)
body: We're not doctors, and this isn't a diagnosis. It's what the research says about a documented overlap that's easy to miss: hypermobility and orthostatic intolerance, including POTS. Miller et al. (2020) examined 91 POTS patients and found that 28 of them, 31%, met the clinical criteria for hEDS.

There's also evidence for a specific mechanism and a specific intervention. A randomized controlled trial by Bourne et al. (JACC, 2021, n=30) tested compression garments during tilt-table testing, which simulates the drop in blood pressure and rise in heart rate that happens on standing. Heart rate during the tilt averaged 109±19 bpm with no compression versus 92±14 bpm with full abdominal and lower-body compression, a statistically significant difference (p<0.001). That's a meaningful reduction in orthostatic tachycardia, and it points to blood pooling in the lower body and abdomen as a real part of what's happening.

sources.text: Bourne et al., JACC 2021, compression and orthostatic tachycardia (n=30)
Miller et al. 2020, hEDS criteria in POTS patients (n=91)

action_title: What to bring to a doctor
action_body: If standing up reliably brings on dizziness or a racing heart, a doctor can check for orthostatic intolerance with a simple standing test or a tilt-table study, and that's worth pursuing alongside any joint hypermobility history. Our POTS-Adjacent Dizziness and Orthostatic Intolerance page covers the fuller picture, including what compression garments and other management approaches the research has looked at.

title: Chronic fatigue that doesn't improve with rest
intro: Feeling exhausted no matter how much sleep you get is one of the most common complaints there is, and it's usually approached through sleep hygiene, stress levels, diet, and ruling out thyroid or iron problems.
Those are reasonable first steps, and they resolve fatigue for a lot of people. When fatigue persists despite all of that, it's worth looking further.

sections.heading: The Hypermobility Link Behind Rest-Resistant Fatigue
body: We're not doctors. Here's a piece of the research that connects fatigue to something most fatigue workups don't check: dysautonomia, meaning dysfunction in the nervous system that regulates blood pressure, heart rate, and related automatic functions.

De Wandele et al. (2014) studied a cohort with the hypermobility type of EDS and found orthostatic intolerance in 74% of that group, compared to 34% of controls. The study also found this correlated with fatigue, pain severity, and reduced quality of life, so the connection isn't incidental.

A separate, larger 2025 study at a single tertiary care center reviewed autonomic testing results for 270 adults with hEDS and found some form of autonomic dysfunction, most of it mild rather than severe, in 90% of patients. Broken down by the specific pattern found on tilt-table testing: 33% met criteria for postural tachycardia syndrome (POTS), 22% for hypocapnic cerebral hypoperfusion, 18% for orthostatic cerebral hyperperfusion syndrome, and 9% for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension. These are distinct, specific diagnoses, not interchangeable labels, which is part of why dysautonomia tied to hEDS can be missed if testing only screens for classic POTS. What both sources agree on is the direction: dysautonomia turns up often in hEDS, and it's tied to the kind of fatigue that doesn't respond to rest alone.

action_title: What to bring to a doctor
action_body: If fatigue hasn't improved despite addressing sleep, iron, and thyroid function, it's worth asking a doctor about screening for dysautonomia or orthostatic intolerance, particularly if there's any history of joint hypermobility. Our Fatigue and Post-Exertional Crash page covers this research in more depth.

sources.text: De Wandele et al., 'Dysautonomia and its underlying mechanisms in the hypermobility type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome,' Seminars in Arthritis and Rheumatism, 2014;44(1):93-100 (n=39 vs. 35 controls)
'Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome: Cerebrovascular, Autonomic and Neuropathic Features,' American Journal of Medicine Open, 2025 (n=270)
